cues.text:
Let’s compare two models on the same
bug. The baseline function accepts zero.

The issue says one and five should pass,
while zero and negative one should fail.

We ask for a cause, a small fix, and one
regression test.

Before opening either chat, write these
expectations down.

That gives both answers the same
standard.

Open the model picker in Copilot Chat.
Choose two options actually available in

your managed workspace and record their
labels.

Use the same session mode for both. If
your account offers one model,

run it twice to see whether the answer
stays consistent.

Record those as two attempts with the
same model.

Use two fresh Plan sessions on the same
revision.

In each, attach the issue, the
validator, and its tests.

Paste the same prompt. Ask why zero
passes,

then request a minimal fix and one
regression test.
Leave edits out of this comparison.

If a run sees more source or uses a
different mode,

record that difference before
interpreting its result.

Example A identifies equality, proposes
a zero test,
and keeps the existing interface.

Example B also finds the cause, but adds
a refactor the issue never asked for.

Both may sound polished. Score the
substance first.

Only then look at the example response
times. Those numbers describe these

illustrative runs and can vary across
attempts and sessions.

For this task, the smaller proposal is
easier to review because the expected
behavior is explicit.

A larger migration may justify
evaluating a stronger reasoning option
on a representative task.

You can make that choice from several
runs and the evidence they produce.

In this small exercise, the best signal
is whether the suggested regression
catches the defect.

Compare two test ideas. A test that
expects one to pass stays green on the
buggy revision.

A test that expects zero to fail exposes
the equality bug.

Run the chosen assertion on the original
code in an approved runner.

Then apply the small fix and repeat the
test. Seeing red first and green

afterward makes the model comparison
concrete.

Write a short decision a teammate can
repeat. Name the two model labels,

the task, the shared inputs, and the
evidence you used.

You might say Example A was easier to
review because it preserved the

signature and produced a test that
failed on the original.

Repeat the comparison on another small
task before treating one result as a
general preference.
